texts.0: SP, due to late recognition of lateral movement while flying fingertip, did not hold the 10 ft minimum lateral separation reference and let the spacing vary without any stabilizing correction. Separation opened past 30 ft on the outside of the turns and on one occasion closed inside the 10 ft reference, which the criteria do not permit in any direction. The IP intervened on the controls to re-establish a safe lateral distance before the next maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to a lateral correction applied with aileron and rudder only after the sight picture had fully widened, allowed lateral separation to reach about 28 to 30 ft, at the outer edge of the tolerance. The deviation was reduced only after verbal prompts from the IP and after the wings had already been rolled level. No control intervention was required, but no correction was initiated by SP alone.
texts.2: SP, due to a lateral correction started after the widening had already begun, let separation grow to roughly 20 to 25 ft during the descending turns. SP recognized the change in the sight picture, applied a small coordinated input toward the leader and re-established the reference within a few seconds. No prompting and no intervention from the IP were needed.
texts.3: SP held lateral separation inside the plus 10 ft tolerance throughout climbs, descents and turns, keeping the working range between 10 and 20 ft from the reference. Corrections were small, early and made with coordinated aileron and rudder. The 10 ft minimum was never eroded on either side of the leader.
texts.4: SP kept lateral separation within a couple of feet of the 10 ft reference through the full profile, including the modified Lazy Eights. Lateral corrections were anticipated from the leader's roll input rather than applied after the picture had changed. The spacing appeared visually constant from the rear cockpit throughout the formation phase.
texts.marginal: SP kept lateral separation inside standards, but worked consistently near the plus 10 ft edge, particularly on the right side and in the second half of each turn. The tendency was toward widening rather than closing, so no safety margin was lost, but the position flown was not the briefed one. SP is expected to narrow the working band back toward the reference line on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP, due to a lateral correction applied with aileron and rudder only after the sight picture had fully widened, worked the fingertip position with lateral separation near 28 to 30 ft, at the outer edge of the tolerance, before the wings were rolled level. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to narrow the working band back toward the reference line.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a lateral correction started after the widening had already begun, let separation grow to about 22 ft during the descending turns before recognizing the change in the sight picture and re-establishing the reference without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to narrow the working band back toward the reference line.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag before the lateral correction was applied, held lateral separation inside the plus 10 ft tolerance throughout climbs, descents and turns, with the working range settling near 15 ft of lateral separation. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to narrow the working band back toward the reference line.

texts_above.2: SP let separation grow to about 22 ft during the descending turns before recognizing the change in the sight picture and applying a small coordinated input toward the leader, re-establishing the reference within a few seconds without prompting. Anticipating the widening from the leader's roll input, rather than after the picture changes, would hold that margin tighter. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good lateral-picture anticipation technique.
texts_above.3: SP held lateral separation inside the plus 10 ft tolerance throughout climbs, descents and turns, with corrections small, early and made with coordinated aileron and rudder. The correction timing is already early through the maneuver set; only the smallest further margin remains. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good lateral-picture anticipation technique.
texts_above.4: SP kept lateral separation within a couple of feet of the 10 ft reference through the full profile, including the modified Lazy Eights, with corrections anticipated from the leader's roll input. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent lateral-picture anticipation technique.

error_modes.label: Vertical separation and stack position as wingman

texts.0: SP, due to unarrested vertical movement in the stack during the pull-up of the Lazy Eight, did not maintain the briefed level of the sight picture. Vertical displacement exceeded 6 ft high and, in the descending portion, more than 10 ft low, beyond the permitted band in both directions. The IP took the controls to reposition the aircraft in the stack.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction combined with a nose-high pitch input, went about 6 ft high over the top and reached the 10 ft low limit during the descending segment. Return to the briefed level came only after repeated verbal calls from the IP. The control combination used was correct, but every correction was made after the displacement had fully developed.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow pitch response to the leader's climb entry, allowed the stack to vary by roughly 5 to 6 ft high and 6 to 8 ft low. SP identified the displacement against the reference on the leader's aircraft and returned to level with a smooth pitch and power correction. No IP prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained the vertical position within 4 ft of the briefed stack through climbs, descents, turns and Lazy Eights. Pitch and power corrections were small and made as the leader's attitude changed rather than after the displacement had built up. The sight picture remained stable in the vertical on both sides.
texts.4: SP held the stack within about 1 to 2 ft of the briefed level for the whole formation phase, including the 2 to 3 G loading and the airspeed variation between 80 and 100 KIAS. Vertical corrections were continuous and small enough to leave the sight picture visually unchanged.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the vertical standards, but settled slightly low in the stack during every descending segment and returned to level only near the wings-level point. The displacement stayed inside 4 ft, so the criteria were met, but the pattern repeated on each maneuver. SP is expected to lead the pitch correction with the leader's nose movement on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP, due to a late power reduction combined with a nose-high pitch input, went about 6 ft high over the top of the Lazy Eight before the stack was corrected back to level. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to lead the pitch correction with the leader's nose movement.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a slow pitch response to the leader's climb entry, let the stack vary to about 5 ft high before identifying the displacement against the reference on the leader's aircraft and returning to level with a smooth pitch and power correction, without prompting. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to lead the pitch correction with the leader's nose movement.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag in the pitch response to the leader's climb entry, maintained the vertical position within 4 ft of the briefed stack through climbs, descents, turns and Lazy Eights, with corrections made as the leader's attitude changed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to lead the pitch correction with the leader's nose movement.

texts_above.2: SP let the stack vary to about 5 ft high before identifying the displacement against the reference on the leader's aircraft and returning to level with a smooth pitch and power correction, without any prompting. Leading the pitch correction with the leader's climb entry itself would hold that variation smaller. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound stack-reference pitch anticipation.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the vertical position within 4 ft of the briefed stack through climbs, descents, turns and Lazy Eights, with pitch and power corrections small and made as the leader's attitude changed rather than after. The stack reference is already stable through most of the maneuver set; only the smallest further margin remains. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed stack-reference pitch anticipation.
texts_above.4: SP held the stack within about 1 to 2 ft of the briefed level for the whole formation phase, including the 2 to 3 G loading and the airspeed variation, with vertical corrections continuous and small. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional stack-reference pitch anticipation.

error_modes.label: Observance angle and fore-aft geometry as wingman

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on the wingtip reference at the expense of the complete sight picture, did not hold the briefed observance angle. The angle swept past 55 deg aft during the turns into the wingman and moved forward of the acute limit on rollout, outside any permitted band. The IP directed the reposition and assisted on the controls to restore the fingertip geometry.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on lateral spacing alone, let the observance angle sweep to about 50 deg, at the widest permitted band. The aft position was reduced only after the IP called the sweep, and SP then over-corrected forward before stabilizing. Power was applied late in each of these corrections.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power addition as the leader rolled into the turn, allowed the observance angle to open to roughly 40 to 45 deg. SP recognized the aft drift from the changing sight picture and used power with a small nose position change to return toward the briefed geometry. The correction was completed without prompting.
texts.3: SP maintained the observance angle within 5 deg of the briefed 30 deg through the full maneuver set. Fore and aft corrections were made with power alone, in small increments, and the geometry was preserved on both sides of the leader.
texts.4: SP held the observance angle essentially constant at the briefed 30 deg, with no visible fore or aft movement during climbs, descents, turns and modified Lazy Eights. Power changes were anticipated from the leader's attitude rather than applied after the sight picture had already moved.
texts.marginal: SP kept the observance angle inside the standard, but worked steadily toward the aft side of the band, near 35 deg, whenever the formation was loaded to 2 to 3 G. The geometry stayed legal and no closure developed, but the position was not the briefed one. SP is expected to hold the nominal angle under G on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP, due to attention held on lateral spacing alone, let the observance angle sweep to about 50 degrees, at the widest permitted band, before it was reduced with power. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the nominal angle under G.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a delayed power addition as the leader rolled into the turn, let the observance angle open to about 42 degrees before recognizing the aft drift from the changing sight picture and using power with a small nose position change to return toward the briefed geometry, without prompting. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to hold the nominal angle under G.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag in adding power as the leader rolled into the turn, maintained the observance angle close to the briefed 30 degrees through the full maneuver set, with fore and aft corrections made by power alone in small increments. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the nominal angle under G.

texts_above.2: SP let the observance angle open to about 42 degrees before recognizing the aft drift from the changing sight picture and using power with a small nose position change, returning toward the briefed geometry without prompting. Adding power as the leader's roll begins, rather than after the picture changes, would hold that drift smaller. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to solid fore-aft power anticipation on the observance angle.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the observance angle close to the briefed 30 degrees through the full maneuver set, with fore and aft corrections made by power alone in small increments on both sides of the leader. The power anticipation already tracks the leader's roll closely; only the smallest lag remains. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to well-developed fore-aft power anticipation on the observance angle.
texts_above.4: SP held the observance angle essentially constant at the briefed 30 degrees, with no visible fore or aft movement during climbs, descents, turns and modified Lazy Eights. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding fore-aft power anticipation on the observance angle.

error_modes.label: Leader smoothness and completion of the planned maneuvers

texts.0: SP, as leader, due to abrupt entries into the planned maneuvers, did not execute or complete them smoothly. Roll and pitch inputs were applied at rates the wingman could not follow, the wingman fell out of the fingertip position and one modified Lazy Eight was abandoned. The IP assumed the lead role to re-form the flight.
texts.1: SP, as leader, due to uneven roll rates at the entry of each turn, completed the planned maneuvers but not smoothly. The wingman had to make large corrections to stay in position, and SP moderated the inputs only after the IP called for a smoother lead. Two maneuvers were flown at a bank and rate other than briefed.
texts.2: SP, as leader, due to an initially rapid roll into the first turn, produced one entry that the wingman had to chase. SP recognized the effect on the wingman's position and flew the remaining climbs, descents and turns at steady, predictable rates. All planned maneuvers were completed as briefed without IP input.
texts.3: SP, as leader, executed and completed all planned maneuvers - climbs, descents, turns and modified Lazy Eights - with smooth and predictable control inputs. Entries and exits were flown at constant rates that allowed the wingman to hold the fingertip position. The briefed profile was completed in full.
texts.4: SP, as leader, flew the whole maneuver set with continuous, low-rate inputs that kept the flight path predictable from the wingman's cockpit. Bank up to 90 deg and airspeed variation between 80 and 100 KIAS were introduced progressively, with no abrupt transition at any point. The wingman remained in fingertip throughout.
texts.marginal: SP, as leader, kept every maneuver within the briefed parameters, but the entries were consistently firmer than the exits, so the wingman worked hardest in the first seconds of each turn. No maneuver had to be repeated and no parameter was exceeded. SP is expected to match entry and exit rates more evenly on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP, due to uneven roll rates at the entry of each turn, completed the planned maneuvers with the wingman making large corrections to stay in position before the inputs were moderated to a smoother rate. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to match entry and exit rates more evenly.
texts_at.2: SP, due to an initially rapid roll into the first turn, produced one entry the wingman had to chase before recognizing the effect on the wingman's position and flying the remaining climbs, descents and turns at steady, predictable rates without prompting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to match entry and exit rates more evenly.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief overshoot of roll rate at the first entry, executed and completed all planned maneuvers with smooth and predictable control inputs, entries and exits flown at constant rates that allowed the wingman to hold the fingertip position. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to match entry and exit rates more evenly.

texts_above.2: SP produced one entry the wingman had to chase before recognizing the effect on the wingman's position and flying the remaining climbs, descents and turns at steady, predictable rates, all planned maneuvers completed as briefed without any input. Matching the entry rate to the exit rate from the first turn would remove that early chase. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady roll-rate consistency as leader.
texts_above.3: SP executed and completed all planned maneuvers with smooth and predictable control inputs, entries and exits flown at constant rates that allowed the wingman to hold the fingertip position throughout. The rates are already close between entry and exit; only the smallest further margin remains. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate roll-rate consistency as leader.
texts_above.4: SP flew the whole maneuver set with continuous, low-rate inputs that kept the flight path predictable, introducing bank and the airspeed variation progressively with no abrupt transition at any point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary roll-rate consistency as leader.

error_modes.label: Leader positive control pressure during Lazy Eight type maneuvers

texts.0: SP, as leader, due to relaxation of back pressure over the top of the modified Lazy Eight, did not maintain positive pressure on the flying controls. The unloading took the loading below the briefed 2 to 3 G range and made the flight path unpredictable, and the wingman lost the fingertip position. The IP intervened to stabilize the maneuver.
texts.1: SP, as leader, due to inconsistent stick pressure through the apex of the Lazy Eights, allowed the loading to fall to the lower edge of the briefed range and the flight path to float. Positive pressure was re-established only after the IP called for it, by which time the wingman was already correcting. The remainder of the profile was flown as briefed.
texts.2: SP, as leader, due to a brief relaxation of back pressure at the first Lazy Eight apex, produced a short unloaded segment that the wingman had to absorb. SP recognized it and maintained continuous positive pressure through the remaining maneuvers, keeping the loading inside the briefed 2 to 3 G band. No IP prompting was required.
texts.3: SP, as leader, maintained positive pressure on the flying controls throughout the Lazy Eight type maneuvers, keeping the loading inside the briefed 2 to 3 G range across each apex. The flight path stayed predictable and the wingman held the fingertip position without large corrections.
texts.4: SP, as leader, held continuous and even control pressure through every Lazy Eight, with no unloaded segment at any apex and airspeed varied smoothly between 80 and 100 KIAS. The resulting flight path allowed the wingman to fly the maneuvers with minimal power changes.
texts.marginal: SP, as leader, kept positive pressure applied through the Lazy Eights, but the loading drifted toward the lower end of the briefed range at each apex. The maneuvers stayed inside the standard and the wingman remained in position. SP is expected to hold the loading more centrally in the 2 to 3 G band on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP, due to inconsistent stick pressure through the apex of the Lazy Eights, let the loading fall to the lower edge of the briefed range and the flight path float before positive pressure was re-established. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the loading more centrally in the 2 to 3 G band.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a brief relaxation of back pressure at the first Lazy Eight apex, produced a short unloaded segment the wingman had to absorb before recognizing it and maintaining continuous positive pressure through the remaining maneuvers, keeping the loading inside the briefed range without prompting. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the loading more centrally in the 2 to 3 G band.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief relaxation of back pressure at the first apex, maintained positive pressure on the flying controls throughout the Lazy Eight type maneuvers, keeping the loading near the briefed 2 to 3 G range across each apex. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold the loading more centrally in the 2 to 3 G band.

texts_above.2: SP produced a short unloaded segment at the first apex that the wingman had to absorb before recognizing it and maintaining continuous positive pressure through the remaining maneuvers, keeping the loading inside the briefed 2 to 3 G band without prompting. Holding continuous pressure through the very first apex would remove that unloaded segment. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable apex control-pressure consistency.
texts_above.3: SP maintained positive pressure on the flying controls throughout the Lazy Eight type maneuvers, keeping the loading inside the briefed 2 to 3 G range across each apex with the flight path staying predictable. The pressure is already continuous through nearly every apex; only the smallest further margin remains. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good apex control-pressure consistency.
texts_above.4: SP held continuous and even control pressure through every Lazy Eight, with no unloaded segment at any apex and airspeed varied smoothly between the briefed values. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior apex control-pressure consistency.

error_modes.label: Leader account of wingman position relative to sun and area borders

texts.0: SP, as leader, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the area boundary, selected the maneuver sequence without regard for the wingman's position. Turns were initiated into the sun with the wingman on the sun side and one maneuver was set up toward the area limit. The IP directed a reversal of the maneuver to keep the flight inside the working area.
texts.1: SP, as leader, due to attention held on own flight parameters, took the wingman's position with respect to the sun and the area borders into account only after the IP prompted. One turn was started with the wingman looking directly into the sun and had to be reversed on call. No area boundary was exceeded.
texts.2: SP, as leader, due to a late assessment of the area geometry, set up one maneuver in a direction that would have placed the wingman on the sun side. SP recognized it before the roll-in, reversed the direction of turn and continued the sequence away from the area border. The correction was made without IP prompting.
texts.3: SP, as leader, considered the wingman's position relative to the sun and the flight area borders before each maneuver and selected the turn directions accordingly. The sequence was flown well inside the area and the wingman was never placed into the sun during a maneuver.
texts.4: SP, as leader, planned the whole sequence around the wingman's position, alternating turn directions to keep the sun behind the formation and using the available area without approaching its limits. Each maneuver was set up before the previous one had been completed.
texts.marginal: SP, as leader, kept the flight inside the area and out of the sun, but the direction of turn was decided close to the roll-in point rather than planned in advance. Nothing was exceeded and the wingman was not placed into the sun. SP is expected to plan the maneuver sequence one maneuver ahead on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP, due to attention held on own flight parameters, took the wingman's position with respect to the sun and area borders into account only after it was raised, with one turn started with the wingman looking into the sun. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to plan the maneuver sequence one maneuver ahead.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a late assessment of the area geometry, set up one maneuver in a direction that would have placed the wingman on the sun side before recognizing it prior to the roll-in, reversing the direction of turn and continuing away from the area border, without prompting. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to plan the maneuver sequence one maneuver ahead.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief delay in assessing the area geometry, considered the wingman's position relative to the sun and the flight area borders before each maneuver, selecting turn directions accordingly with the sequence flown well inside the area. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to plan the maneuver sequence one maneuver ahead.

texts_above.2: SP set up one maneuver in a direction that would have placed the wingman on the sun side before recognizing it prior to the roll-in, reversing the direction of turn and continuing the sequence away from the area border, without prompting. Planning the turn direction one maneuver ahead, rather than assessing it at the roll-in, would remove that reversal. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to assured sequence-planning awareness of wingman position.
texts_above.3: SP considered the wingman's position relative to the sun and the flight area borders before each maneuver and selected the turn directions accordingly, with the sequence flown well inside the area. The area assessment already precedes each roll-in; only the smallest further margin remains. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to precise sequence-planning awareness of wingman position.
texts_above.4: SP planned the whole sequence around the wingman's position, alternating turn directions to keep the sun behind the formation and using the available area without approaching its limits. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate sequence-planning awareness of wingman position.

error_modes.label: Wingman control smoothness, power handling and trim

texts.0: SP, due to stress that produced a tight grip and continuous input in the close position, did not control the aircraft in a smooth and solid way. Corrections were abrupt in all three axes, power was moved in large steps and the aircraft was flown out of trim for the whole formation phase. The resulting oscillation reached the point where the IP had to take control.
texts.1: SP, due to tension on the controls in the close position, made corrections that were larger and later than the deviations called for. Power was used in coarse steps and trim was reset only after the IP called for it, so the position was held with continuous stick force. The position limits were met, but the aircraft was not flown in a solid way.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially firm grip on the stick during the first turns, produced corrections larger than needed and left the aircraft out of trim in pitch. SP recognized the effort required, relaxed the inputs, retrimmed and flew the remaining maneuvers with smooth power and small corrections. No IP prompting was required.
texts.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way with no abrupt corrections, used engine power in small proportional increments and trimmed continuously as airspeed changed. The fingertip position determined in the Techniques and Procedures Manual was preserved throughout the maneuver set.
texts.4: SP flew the close position with inputs small enough to be imperceptible from the leader's cockpit, matching power to the leader's changes as they developed and keeping the aircraft trimmed through the 80 to 100 KIAS variation. The fingertip position was preserved with no visible correction at any point.
texts.marginal: SP flew smoothly and kept the position within standards, but retrimmed only after each airspeed change rather than during it, so part of the profile was flown against residual stick force. Corrections stayed small and no parameter was exceeded. SP is expected to trim continuously with the airspeed change on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP, due to tension on the controls in the close position, made corrections larger and later than the deviations called for before power was used in smaller steps and trim was reset. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to trim continuously with the airspeed change.
texts_at.2: SP, due to an initially firm grip on the stick during the first turns, produced corrections larger than needed and left the aircraft out of trim in pitch at first before recognizing the effort required, relaxing the inputs, retrimming and flying the remaining maneuvers with smooth power and small corrections, without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to trim continuously with the airspeed change.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief firmness of grip during the first turns, controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way with corrections small for nearly the whole maneuver set, using engine power in small proportional increments and trimming as airspeed changed. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to trim continuously with the airspeed change.

texts_above.2: SP produced corrections larger than needed and left the aircraft out of trim in pitch at first before recognizing the effort required, relaxing the inputs, retrimming and flying the remaining maneuvers with smooth power and small corrections, without prompting. Relaxing the grip from the first turn, rather than partway through, would remove that early over-control. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent close-position grip and trim discipline.
texts_above.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way with no abrupt corrections, using engine power in small proportional increments and trimming continuously as airspeed changed. The technique is already smooth with power handled in small increments; only the smallest trim lag remains. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined close-position grip and trim discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the close position with inputs small enough to be imperceptible from the leader's cockpit, matching power to the leader's changes as they developed and keeping the aircraft trimmed through the airspeed variation. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless close-position grip and trim discipline.

error_modes.label: Speed brake use and overtake control from both sides

texts.0: SP, due to failure to recognize developing overtake, did not use the speed brake when it was required to keep closure under control. The speed brake was left retracted through an accelerating closure from the left side and was then extended fully with the leader's aircraft already filling the sight picture. The IP intervened with power and speed brake to stop the closure.
texts.1: SP, due to a late assessment of the closure rate, extended the speed brake only after the IP called for it and, on one occasion, left it extended after the overtake had been stopped, producing an aft drift. The leader's speed brake command was actioned with a noticeable delay. Closure was regained without intervention on the controls.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power reduction as the leader decelerated, developed a moderate overtake from the right side. SP recognized the closure, extended the speed brake, retracted it as the geometry stabilized and returned to position with power. No prompting or intervention from the IP was required.
texts.3: SP used the speed brake from both sides on the leader's command and whenever it was needed to keep overtake under control. Extension and retraction were timed to the closure rate and combined with proportional power changes, so the position was regained without overshoot.
texts.4: SP anticipated closure from the leader's attitude and power changes and used the speed brake only where power alone would not have been sufficient, on both the left and the right side. Every extension was matched by a timely retraction and no overtake was allowed to develop.
texts.marginal: SP used the speed brake correctly on command and stopped every overtake inside the position limits, but on the right side the extension was consistently later than on the left. No closure became significant and the position was preserved. SP is expected to apply the same timing from both sides on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP, due to a late assessment of the closure rate, extended the speed brake only after it was called for and, on one occasion, left it extended after the overtake had stopped, producing an aft drift before it was regained. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the same timing from both sides.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a delayed power reduction as the leader decelerated, developed a moderate overtake from the right side at first before recognizing the closure, extending the speed brake, retracting it as the geometry stabilized and returning to position with power, without prompting. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to apply the same timing from both sides.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag in reducing power as the leader decelerated, used the speed brake from both sides on the leader's command and whenever needed to keep overtake under control, with extension and retraction timed to the closure rate. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to apply the same timing from both sides.

texts_above.2: SP developed a moderate overtake from the right side at first before recognizing the closure, extending the speed brake, retracting it as the geometry stabilized and returning to position with power, without prompting. Extending the speed brake with the same timing on the right as on the left would remove that early overtake. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to good speed-brake side-symmetry technique.
texts_above.3: SP used the speed brake from both sides on the leader's command and whenever it was needed to keep overtake under control, with extension and retraction timed to the closure rate and combined with proportional power changes. The timing is already close between the two sides; only the smallest asymmetry remains. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good speed-brake side-symmetry technique.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated closure from the leader's attitude and power changes and used the speed brake only where power alone would not have been sufficient, on both the left and the right side, with every extension matched by a timely retraction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent speed-brake side-symmetry technique.

error_modes.label: Correcting one reference at a time instead of all axes together

texts.0: SP, due to attempting to correct vertical, fore-aft and lateral deviations simultaneously instead of one reference at a time, never re-established any of the three fingertip references. The stack ran past 10 ft low, the observance angle swept beyond the aft limit and the spacing closed inside the 10 ft lateral reference during the same turn. The IP took the controls to rebuild the fingertip position before the next maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to working two references at once rather than in the sequence stack, fore-aft, lateral, allowed deviations to reach the outer limits at about 6 ft high in the stack and near 30 ft of lateral spacing. The picture stabilized only after repeated IP calls to set the stack first and leave the spacing alone. No control intervention was needed, but the correction order was never adopted by SP alone.
texts.2: SP, due to one combined pitch and bank correction on the first turn, let the stack run about 6 ft low while the spacing opened to roughly 20 ft. error_modes.label: Chasing the power and over-control of the PCL

texts.0: SP, due to chasing the power with large PCL displacements instead of the three small movements that start, stop and stabilize the aircraft, never damped the fore-aft oscillation in the close position. Each correction produced an overshoot in the opposite direction, the observance angle swung between well aft and acute and closure toward the leader developed twice. The IP intervened on the throttle and controls to stop the oscillation.
texts.1: SP, due to power corrections made with whole-arm movements rather than small wrist inputs, over-corrected on nearly every fore-aft deviation and let the observance angle reach the widest permitted band before reversing. The oscillation was damped only after the IP called for smaller power steps. Position limits were held, but the aircraft was never stabilized with the third, settling power movement.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial power addition larger than the aft displacement required, overshot forward and had to reduce power again on the first two corrections. SP recognized the chasing pattern, changed to small wrist movements and began using a second movement to stop the aircraft and a third to stabilize it. Deviations stayed in the middle band and no prompting was required.
texts.3: SP made each power correction with three distinct PCL movements, one to start the correction, one to stop the aircraft and one to stabilize it in the desired position. Fore-aft deviations were contained within the code 3 geometry and no correction produced an overshoot in the opposite direction. Power was moved with the wrist rather than the whole arm throughout.
texts.4: SP matched every power correction to the size of the deviation, so the start, stop and stabilize movements were barely perceptible and the aircraft settled without any reversal of PCL direction. No fore-aft oscillation developed at any point of the profile, including the airspeed variation between 80 and 100 KIAS.
texts.marginal: SP applied the three-movement power technique and stayed inside the standards, but the initial movement was consistently slightly larger than needed, so a small reduction was always required to stop the aircraft. texts.2: SP, due to an incorrect initial reference on rejoin, set the pitot tube rather than the aft wingtip light against the exhaust stack opening and flew about 5 ft out of the briefed line. texts.3: SP flew the close position on the briefed references, placing the exhaust stack on top of the leader's closest wing for the vertical, centering the aft wingtip light on the front edge of the exhaust stack opening for the fore-aft, and aligning with the forward edge of the horizontal stabilizer for the lateral. texts.4: SP acquired all three briefed references immediately on arriving in the close position and used them consistently from both the left and the right side, with the pitot tube kept on the aft edge of the exhaust stack opening. error_modes.label: Leader roll rate continuity - stair-stepping and roll reversal

texts.0: SP, as leader, due to stair-stepped and ratcheted roll rates into and out of the turns, did not provide a stable platform for the wingman. texts.2: SP, as leader, due to a ratcheted roll rate at the first roll-in, produced one entry the wingman had to chase before settling. texts.4: SP, as leader, flew the complete exercise with continuous roll rates, blending pitch with roll at each entry and reversing direction while maintaining positive G, so the wingman never had to reset a correction mid-roll. error_modes.label: Wingman handling of lag pursuit in turns away and turns into

texts.0: SP, as wingman, due to failing to add back pressure and power in the lag pursuit position of a turn away, did not climb with the leader and the stack collapsed well below the permitted band. On the following turn into, no forward pressure or power reduction was applied and the aircraft moved high and forward with closure toward the leader. The IP intervened on the controls to restore separation.
texts.1: SP, as wingman, due to back pressure applied without the accompanying power increase in the turns away, arrived at the low limit of the vertical band and hung aft in the geometry. The required power was added only after the IP called for it, and the power reduction at the completion of the relative climb came late enough to leave the aircraft forward. Limits were held, but every correction followed the deviation.
texts.2: SP, as wingman, due to a late recognition of the lag pursuit position at the first turn away, allowed the stack to fall about 6 ft low before increasing back pressure and power. SP identified the pattern, climbed with the leader on the following leaves and reduced power as the relative climb was completed. In the turns into, forward pressure with a power reduction was applied without prompting.
